query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In chromium‐rich steels for chemical processing and nuclear power applications, enhanced corrosion resistance is primarily achieved via the formation of a stable, self-healing Cr2O3-rich passive film whose kinetics are further accelerated by a refined microstructure (e.g., high grain boundary density) that rapidly supplies Cr to damaged areas.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional high-Cr stainless or duplex steel in a coarse-grained, as-received state with standard bulk composition.
generation.intervention: Heat treatment and/or thermo-mechanical processing to induce a finer grain structure and alter grain boundary character coupled with controlled minor alloying (if needed) to optimize Cr availability at the surface.
generation.conditions: Exposure to aggressive environments representative of chemical-processing media (e.g., chloride-containing aqueous solutions or molten salts) and simulated nuclear power operating conditions (elevated temperatures with potential irradiation effects), with experiments performed under controlled electrochemical testing conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The microstructural features (e.g., increased grain boundary area) that enable accelerated diffusion of Cr to the surface, supporting the formation and repair of the Cr2O3 passive layer.
generation.mechanism: The enhanced grain boundary network and optimized alloying allow for rapid formation and reformation of a dense Cr2O3-rich film that acts as a barrier to corrosive species, reducing the dissolution rate of the underlying metal. In aggressive media, the passive film may also act as a redox buffer, lowering the local corrosion kinetics.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to coarse-grained steels, the fine-grained, microstructure‐engineered steels will exhibit lower corrosion current densities, slower passive film breakdown, and reduced depth of corrosive attack, measured by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and surface analysis (e.g., XPS) that reveals a thicker and more uniform Cr2O3-rich layer.
generation.baseline: Standard coarse-grained high-Cr stainless or duplex steels without additional grain refinement or microstructural modification, showing a conventional passivation behavior.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for steels where the Cr content is above the critical threshold for passivation (typically ≥ 12–15 wt.% Cr) and under environmental conditions that permit the formation and stability of the oxide film; extreme irradiation or mechanical damage might alter diffusion kinetics and passivation behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative effect of grain refinement on the kinetics of Cr diffusion and passive film repair under irradiation conditions remains uncertain; potential interactions with other alloying elements in multi-component steels may also modulate the overall corrosion response.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-Cr steels with identical chemical compositions. One set will be processed to achieve a refined microstructure with high grain boundary density (via controlled thermo-mechanical processing), while the other set remains coarse-grained. Expose both sets to identical aggressive environments (e.g., 0.6 M NaCl solution at elevated temperature or a molten salt environment simulating nuclear power conditions). Monitor corrosion behavior over time with electrochemical measurements coupled with surface analysis.
measurements: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and potentiodynamic polarization to measure corrosion current densities and passivation behavior.
Surface characterization tools (XPS, SEM) to assess the thickness, composition, and uniformity of the passive film, specifically the content and distribution of Cr2O3.
Cross-sectional microscopy to evaluate corrosion penetration depth.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the refined microstructure steels do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in corrosion resistance (i.e., no lower corrosion current density, no thicker or more uniform Cr2O3 layer, and similar or greater penetration depth) compared to the coarse-grained baseline, then the hypothesized mechanism—that enhanced passive film formation via grain boundary–mediated Cr diffusion is responsible for resistance—is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Early research reported that stainless steel, Fe-Cr alloy, and CrFe15Ni15 alloy have excellent corrosion resistance due to the dense Cr2O3 passivation film formed on the surface [,,]. Similarly, it was speculated that the Cr2O3 passivation film has the same effect in the corrosion resistance of HEAs. AlCoCrFeNi [], AlxCrFe1.5MnNi0.5 [], and Al0.5CoCrCuFeNiBx [] verified the foregoing speculation. Therefore, for the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating passivation film of this study, it can be obtained from the results of XPS that the Cr2O3 in the passivation film provides good corrosion resistance for the coating, and the addition of trace amount of Nb results in forming a stable metal oxide of Nb2O5 in the passivation film of the coating, which also plays a positive role in the corrosion resistance [,].

cited_evidence.kind: web:4.1. Effect of Alloy Composition on Molten Salt Corrosion Behavior
cited_evidence.text: Cr depletion depth increased significantly in DS2205 compared to AlCoCrFeNi2.1, with an increase in temperature from 450 °C to 650 °C. At 650 °C, the Cr depletion depth for AlCoCrFeNi2.1 was ~50 μm, while that for DS2205 was ~300 μm. This suggests that Al in the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 acted as a sacrificial element and reduced Cr dissolution rate in the molten salt compared to DS2205. Redox control technique has been utilized for corrosion mitigation in molten fluoride and chloride salts []. Dissolution of Al and Cr into the molten salt resulted in the formation of AlCl3 and CrCl2, which formed a redox couple of Al/AlCl3 and Cr/CrCl2. At the redox potential, Co, Ni, and Fe become relatively nobler and their dissolution is thermodynamically unfavorable. These findings suggest that Al/AlCl3 and Cr/CrCl2 couple may be used as redox buffer to slow or stop the dissolution of Fe, Co, and Ni from AlCoCrFeNi2.1 [].
